theorem_title: A transitive composite forces a common invariant to be constant
natural_language_statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be arbitrary types, let $I:X\to Y$, and let $A,A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime}:X\to X$ satisfy the right-inverse identities $A(A^{\prime}(x))=x$ and $B(B^{\prime}(x))=x$ for every $x\in X$. Assume $I(A(x))=I(x)$ and $I(B(x))=I(x)$ for every $x$. Put $F=B^{\prime}\circ A^{\prime}\circ B\circ A$, and suppose every $y\in X$ can be reached from every $x\in X$ by some nonnegative iterate: $\forall x,y\ \exists n\in\mathbb N,\ F^n(x)=y$. Then

$$\forall x,y\in X,\qquad I(x)=I(y).$$

Here $F^0$ is the identity map. This general invariance principle is the formal core used by the residue-first-integral argument. The theorem assumes neither finiteness of $X$ nor left-inverse laws, and it does not itself supply the arithmetic residue-model construction.
formal_statement:
theorem CollatzWork.Disproof.FiniteResidueFirstIntegral.commutator_transitive_forces_constant
    {X Color : Type} (I : X → Color)
    (A Ainv B Binv : X → X)
    (hARightInverse : ∀ x, A (Ainv x) = x)
    (hBRightInverse : ∀ x, B (Binv x) = x)
    (hA : IsInvariant I A) (hB : IsInvariant I B)
    (htransitive : ∀ x y, ∃ n,
      iterate (commutator A Ainv B Binv) n x = y) :
    ∀ x y, I x = I y := by sorry
